lessons.title: Twentieth-Century Colour: Orchestration, Dynamics and Space

before.description: How composers writing after 1910 used tone colour, spacing, long-range dynamics, jazz influence and the wind band to build a new twentieth-century sound world.
before.content_html:
A New Sound World

Before 1910, most classical music built its effect from melody, harmony and rhythm, in that order. Tone colour mattered, but it served the tune underneath it. After 1910, many composers began treating timbre itself as a subject worth composing with, not just a wrapper around a melody. The choice of instrument became part of the musical idea, not an afterthought.

This shows up first in orchestration. Composers picked unusual instrument pairings, extreme registers and exposed solo colours precisely because of how they sounded, not just because of the notes they played. A phrase given to a bassoon high in its range, or to a solo flute over hushed strings, means something different from the same phrase given to a full string section — even if every pitch is identical.

Key Fact

The same melody can sound completely different depending on which instrument plays it, how loudly, and how many other parts surround it — twentieth-century composers built entire pieces around exploiting this.

Open Space versus Dense Texture

Composers also began treating texture as an expressive choice in its own right. A texture can be widely spaced and open — a single melodic line with only a few sustained notes underneath, and a wide gap between the highest and lowest parts — or dense and layered, with many independent lines crowding the same registers at once. Neither approach is better than the other; each creates a completely different sound world, and composers moved between them for contrast.

Long-Range Control of Dynamics

Twentieth-century composers also stretched dynamics to extremes, and controlled them over long spans of time rather than just from phrase to phrase. Instead of one sudden forte, a passage might begin at the edge of audibility and build, bar by bar, across several minutes, in one continuous crescendo towards a huge climax. That long-range shape is itself a structural device, not just a passing effect — it can hold an entire movement together.

Jazz and Popular Idioms Enter the Concert Hall

Jazz and blues, both new popular styles in the early twentieth century, fed directly into concert music. Composers borrowed sliding pitches, bent notes and syncopated rhythms from jazz players and wrote them straight into orchestral scores. A blue note or a smooth upward slide can bring a whole jazz atmosphere into a symphony orchestra without a single jazz musician on stage.

The Wind Band as a Serious Concert Medium

The wind band had long existed for marches and military occasions. In the twentieth century, composers began writing original concert works for it, treating it as a serious medium with its own palette of colours — bright massed brass, reedy woodwind choirs, a full percussion section — rather than as a cheaper substitute for a full orchestra.

Loosening Tonality

Traditional tonal music treats dissonance as tension that must resolve to consonance. After 1910, many composers loosened this rule. Harmony often still points to a home key, but it can be extended tonality: chords built from added and stacked notes, not just plain triads. Others turned to modal scales borrowed from folk music or earlier eras for a different flavour entirely. Crucially, dissonance itself became a colour to enjoy, not a problem that always needed fixing.

Not quite. Fully atonal music, including twelve-note serialism, abandons a home key altogether. Extended tonality and modality are gentler: the music still points towards a tonal centre, but reaches it by a wider, more colourful route than strict major-minor harmony allows.

Putting the Picture Together

When an unfamiliar extract from this period comes up in the exam, run through these five clues. Is timbre doing more than decorating a tune? Is the texture wide open or densely packed? Are the dynamics building over a long span rather than jumping suddenly? Is there any trace of jazz or blues? Could the forces be a wind band rather than a full orchestra? And does the harmony still feel tonal, even though it does not behave like a textbook major or minor key? Naming two or three of these, with the correct technical term, is worth more marks than a general impression.
before.exam_tip_html: In Section A, name the element, give the correct technical term, and say exactly where in the extract you heard it — for example “the dynamics build gradually from very quiet to loud across the whole extract”, not just “it gets louder”. Vague impressions score no marks; precise vocabulary does.

before.description: How Bartók's folk-song collecting shaped Hungarian Sketches, and what to know about the cimbalom, snap rhythms, and the four movements on your AQA specification.
before.content_html:
Bartók, the folk-song collector

Béla Bartók did not just compose from imagination. From 1906 he travelled through remote villages in Hungary and Romania, and later further afield, with a phonograph, recording peasants singing their oldest songs. He and his friend Zoltán Kodály wrote thousands of these melodies down by hand, comparing versions and sorting them by type.

How fieldwork changed his music

That fieldwork changed his own composing. Village singers rarely used the plain major or minor scales of a piano lesson. Bartók heard old modal scales, short phrases repeated and varied rather than developed at length, and rhythms locked to the steps of a dance. All three habits carried straight into his own concert music, including Hungarian Sketches.

Bartók grouped the tunes he collected into an “old style” — pentatonic, freely sung, without regular bar lines — and a “new style” shaped by newer dance forms with a steadier beat. Hungarian Sketches draws on both: slow, speech-like rubato melody in one movement, driving dance rhythm in the next.

Hungarian Sketches: five pictures, four for your exam

Hungarian Sketches, Magyar Képek, or “Hungarian Pictures”, is an orchestral suite Bartók put together in 1931 from five short piano pieces he had written roughly twenty years earlier. Each movement is a small “picture” of Hungarian rural life — a village at dusk, a dance, a drunk stumbling home.

The four movements you need

Key Fact

Your exam asks for four of the five movements: 1 Evening in the Village, 2 Bear Dance, 4 Slightly Tipsy, and 5 Swineherd’s Dance. Movement 3, Melody, is not on the specification — do not spend revision time on it.

Orchestration with a light touch

Hungarian Sketches is written for orchestra — woodwind including piccolo, bass clarinet and contrabassoon, horns, trumpets, trombones and tuba, timpani, percussion including side drums, triangle, cymbals and bass drum, and strings — but used with a light touch.

Evening in the Village uses only woodwind, two horns and strings. Bartók keeps much of the texture thin, often just a solo woodwind line over a handful of accompanying instruments, so each “picture” keeps the intimate feel of a folk tune rather than a big symphonic statement.

Precision about sonority

What examiners reward here is Bartók’s precision about sonority. The strings switch constantly between bowed playing and pizzicato, add fast tremolo for shimmer, play muted (con sordino) and are even asked to play ruvido — coarsely.

The brass mute and unmute; the triangle player is told to use a metal beater. Almost every note of the woodwind melodies carries an articulation instruction. That level of detailed instruction about instrumental colour and dynamics is a signature of the piece — and a ready-made Section B answer.

Snap rhythms and folk-dance patterns

A snap rhythm is a very short, accented note followed by a longer one. It gives a dance an off-balance, kicking feel.

It comes straight from the rhythm of spoken Hungarian and of Hungarian folk dance steps. The dance movements drive differently — on short repeated ostinato figures that keep the dance driving forward.

Evening in the Village (Movement 1)

The movement is in arch form — A, B, A1, B1, A2 — a symmetry Bartók was known for. The A sections are marked Lento rubato, slow and speech-like. The B sections are Allegretto, nearly twice the speed.

A1 brings the slow music back varied, B1 the quick music with trills added, and A2 closes the arch. It is mostly 4/4, but bars of 3/4 and 2/4 near the end unsettle the ending.

Evening in the Village: mode, melody and texture

Both melodies come from the F sharp minor pentatonic scale, and the A section uses the Aeolian mode on F sharp. Both were typical of the folk music Bartók collected.

The A melody is mainly a descending legato phrase — the musical equivalent of a sigh at the end of the day. The B melody is the opposite: staccato, conjunct quavers over short pizzicato, so not everyone’s evening is calm.

Texture is melody and accompaniment, with different woodwind taking the solo line over chordal accompaniment — either long held notes or pizzicato crotchets. Dynamics run from ppp to forte. Bartók avoids traditional cadences and uses non-functional chords, so the key stays deliberately unclear.

Bear Dance (Movement 2)

Bartók described this movement as the impression of a bear dancing to its leader’s song, growling to a drum. It is in varied strophic form, and the easiest way to hear the sections is to follow the pedal note.

A sits on a D pedal in cellos, basses, horns and tuba. B moves the pedal to A flat in the second violins — D to A flat is a tritone. Then A1, B1 and A2 complete the symmetry. The movement ends on a D major chord.

Bear Dance: mode, forces and rhythm

The melody of A is based on the Aeolian mode on D sharp; B uses the Lydian dominant scale on D. Phrases are mostly four bars long and deliberately dissonant, which is what gives the dance its excitement.

Bartók adds two trumpets, two trombones, tuba, contrabassoon, timpani and two side drums to the forces of the first movement. The side drums start without snares and switch them on for B. A triangle appears in A1, the brass sometimes play muted, and the strings both bow and pluck.

Bear Dance: texture and rhythm

Texture revolves around the pedal notes, which act as a rhythmic drone. The melody is harmonised in thirds, sixths and octaves and moves in block chords. Repeated quavers in the pedal and snare drum build the anticipation, while the melody moves mainly in crotchets — the rhythm of the Hungarian kanász folk dance. Dynamics run from piano to forte with sforzando stabs, and there is a great deal of staccato.

Slightly Tipsy (Movement 4)

True to its title, this movement portrays someone stumbling rather than walking in a straight line. It is in ternary form: an opening A section, a contrasting B section, then a return of A that is significantly developed rather than simply repeated.

Almost every note of the opening melody is decorated with acciaccaturas — the single feature that most creates the tipsy feel. The opening melody is built on the interval of a perfect fourth; the second motif descends by step.

Slightly Tipsy: sound and texture

Sonority is mostly woodwind and strings. The strings sometimes play col legno, and at the start they are muted and told to play at the tip of the bow for a thin, quiet sound.

Tonality is deliberately ambiguous. It begins major, and the B section moves to G minor, with parallel chords, chromatic harmony and dissonant added-note chords.

The marking is Allegretto rubato, so the music speeds up and slows down. It is mostly 4/4, but a few bars of 2/4 and one bar of 5/4 unsettle the phrasing. Dynamics run from pianissimo to forte with sudden changes, and slur-staccato articulation makes the music sway.

Swineherd’s Dance (Movement 5)

The suite ends with the only genuine collected folk tune in it. Bartók recorded it in Tolna County in 1907. This movement has more sections than any other here. It opens with an introduction over a drone, with fragments of the tune appearing before it properly arrives.

The first half of the folk melody enters, then the second half. Both halves come back changed: a reworked second half, a four-bar link, then the first half again. After a three-bar link the second half is fragmented and developed, with its final two bars held back — the coda is built on exactly those two bars.

Swineherd’s Dance: mode and sound

The tonal centre is A, set by the drone, and the mode is mixolydian on A. The B section shifts its drone to D before returning to A, and G sharps in its second half lean towards G major.

The melody opens with leaps of fourths and fifths, then moves by step, and sits quite high. The woodwind carry it — piccolo, flute, oboe and clarinet — over strings playing both bowed and pizzicato, muted and unmuted. At the very end two solo violins play harmonics.

Swineherd’s Dance: metre and rhythm

The metre is 2/4 throughout and the marking is Allegro molto: quick and lively, with moments of calm and changes of tempo. An ostinato rhythm — quaver, crotchet, quaver — drives many sections, and the horns and trumpets have syncopated melodies. Dynamics run from pianissimo to fortissimo with many crescendos and diminuendos.

Writing about Hungarian Sketches in Section B

Section B marks come from three things, in this order: name the musical element or technique, give the correct technical term for it, and say exactly where in the movement it happens. “Bartók uses folk music” earns nothing on its own. “Bartók builds the Allegretto dance tune of Evening in the Village on scotch-snap rhythms” earns marks, because it names the feature, uses the right term, and locates it.

Practise building answers in that order for each of the four required movements, and keep the ostinato and scotch-snap vocabulary ready — and make sure each one is attached to the right movement.

glossary_terms.definition: A scale built from a pattern of tones and semitones other than major or minor, often drawn from folk melody.
A scale using only five notes, common in older Hungarian folk melody.
A Hungarian folk instrument, a large trapezoid box of strings struck with small beaters, giving a bright, ringing sound.
A rhythmic figure of a very short, accented note followed by a longer note.
A short musical pattern repeated persistently, often in the bass or accompaniment.
A flexible, expressive stretching and easing of tempo, without a strict beat.
A string technique of plucking the string with a finger instead of using the bow.
A rapid repetition of a single note, or a quick alternation between two notes.
A sustained note or chord held underneath a melody, common in folk music.
Someone who travels to record and write down traditional songs, usually sung from memory rather than read from a page.

before.exam_tip_html: In Section B, never just say “Bartók uses folk music.” Name the actual feature — modal scale, snap rhythm, cimbalom-effect, ostinato — give it its correct term, and say which movement it is in. Marks come from the term and the location, not from a general impression.

flashcard_questions.a: An orchestral suite of five short pictures of Hungarian rural life, put together in 1931 from piano pieces written about twenty years earlier.
flashcard_questions.q: What is Hungarian Sketches, and when did Bartók assemble it?

flashcard_questions.a: 1 Evening in the Village, 2 Bear Dance, 4 Slightly Tipsy and 5 Swineherd's Dance. Movement 3, Melody, is not required.
flashcard_questions.q: Which four movements does your exam require?

flashcard_questions.a: A very short accented note followed by a longer one. It drives the quicker Allegretto dance tune of Evening in the Village.
flashcard_questions.q: What is a snap rhythm, and where is its home in this suite?

flashcard_questions.a: On a near-constant even-quaver ostinato — heavy, staccato, marcato, with sforzando stabs — and after all that force it ends quietly: a deliberate surprise.
flashcard_questions.q: How is Bear Dance built, and how does it end?

flashcard_questions.a: A genuine collected folk tune over driving dance rhythms; a fortissimo climax in the middle of the movement, a long calmo wind-down to pianissimo, then five final bars snap back for one last loud chord.
flashcard_questions.q: Describe the shape of Swineherd's Dance.

before.description: How Adams, Reich and Riley build music from a steady pulse and short repeated cells through the additive process, phasing and layering, and how to spot minimalism in an unfamiliar extract.
before.content_html:
Minimalism: process instead of themes

Minimalism is one of the four listening strands in Area of Study 4. In the exam you might hear an unfamiliar extract and have to recognise it as minimalism within seconds, so you need to know what the technique actually sounds like, not just its name.

Area of Study 1 trained you to listen for themes and their development in sonata form. Minimalism works the opposite way: there is no theme to develop. A composer sets up a short musical idea and a rule for changing it, then lets that rule run. The structure you hear is the process itself, not a plot of themes coming and going.

Key Fact

Minimalism builds pieces from a steady pulse and short repeated cells, changed by a process such as addition or phasing, instead of from themes that are stated and developed.

Every minimalist extract you hear rests on two constants: a pulse that never lets up, and a cell — a short pattern repeated over and over. Everything else in this lesson is a way of changing that cell over time.

Adams, Reich and Riley are all in copyright, so the links below open official recordings on the performers’ or label’s own channels rather than audio hosted here.

The additive process, and how In C differs — Terry Riley

In an additive process, a cell grows by one note at a time: play it, add a note, play the new version, add another note, and the pattern lengthens in front of you. Terry Riley’s In C works differently — built not on note-by-note growth but on staggered repetition. It is not one fixed melody but 53 short numbered patterns; every player in the ensemble repeats each pattern as many times as they like before moving to the next, so the players drift in and out of step with each other and no two performances ever match.

A performance of In C typically runs anywhere from forty-five to ninety minutes — far too long for a revision session. Play a few minutes instead, with the additive process in mind.

  • Terry Riley, In C (Bang on a Can All-Stars) — each player moves through the 53 numbered patterns at their own pace, so listen for the ensemble sliding in and out of alignment as a result.

Phasing and gradual change — Steve Reich

Steve Reich’s signature technique is phasing: two players start an identical pattern together, then one very gradually pulls ahead until the two lines lock into a new relationship. Reich built entire pieces from this single idea. In large ensemble works such as Music for 18 Musicians, that same instinct for extremely gradual, almost imperceptible change is stretched across a much bigger canvas: pulsing chords, tuned percussion parts that interlock note against note in a technique called hocket, and a very slow harmonic rhythm that only shifts every few minutes.

Music for 18 Musicians runs to roughly an hour, so do not attempt the whole piece. Pick any five minutes and listen for how little happens, and how gradually it happens — that slowness is the point, not a flaw.

  • Steve Reich, Music for 18 Musicians — sample any five minutes and notice how little changes, and how gradually it changes.

Layering and texture — John Adams

A minimalist texture rarely arrives all at once. Layer after layer is added on top of the pulse, thickening the sound until a listener notices the piece has quietly built from a bare few instruments into a full ensemble. This layering is easiest to hear when a piece is short enough to take in whole. John Adams’ Short Ride in a Fast Machine lasts about four minutes, which makes it the most immediately graspable of the three pieces in this lesson and a good place to start.

  • John Adams, Short Ride in a Fast Machine (Berliner Philharmoniker) — at under four minutes this is the clearest introduction to the whole technique, so start here before the longer pieces.

Sonata form states a theme, develops it through fragmentation and key change, then restates it. Minimalism states a cell, changes it through a process such as addition or phasing, and lets that process — not a return to the opening idea — carry the structure. If an extract has a clear tune that comes back transformed, think sonata form. If it has a short pattern repeating and mutating with almost no melody to speak of, think minimalism.

Why this matters in the exam

Section A of the listening exam plays short unfamiliar extracts and asks you to identify and describe what you hear. Marks come from naming the element, giving the correct technical term, and saying where in the extract it happened — not from a vague impression that the music “sounds repetitive”. Write “additive process” or “phasing”, not “it keeps going”.

practice_questions.text: Name the technique in which a short pattern grows by one note at a time with each repeat, and explain how Terry Riley's In C creates its shifting textures differently.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for 'additive process'. 1 mark for explaining that In C works differently: its 53 numbered patterns are fixed, and each player repeats one as often as they choose, so the ensemble drifts in and out of alignment rather than a pattern growing note by note.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens in Steve Reich's phasing technique.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for two identical parts starting together. 1 mark for one part gradually shifting out of time with the other, creating new patterns.

practice_questions.text: Compare how structure is created in sonata form and in minimalism.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for sonata form stating a theme; 1 mark for sonata form developing and restating that theme; 1 mark for minimalism using a short repeated cell or pattern; 1 mark for minimalism changing that cell through a process such as addition or phasing rather than developing a theme.

practice_questions.text: Explain how layering contributes to the texture of a minimalist piece.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that instrumental or vocal layers are added one at a time. 1 mark for noting that the texture thickens gradually. 1 mark for linking this to a named example or the effect on the listener, such as building from a bare texture to a full ensemble.

practice_questions.text: State two features you would expect to hear in an unfamiliar minimalist extract.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: steady, unchanging pulse; short repeated cell or pattern; slow harmonic rhythm; gradual layering or textural build; note-against-note (hocket) interlocking on tuned percussion. Accept other valid minimalist features.

practice_questions.text: A student says minimalist music 'just repeats without doing anything'. Using named examples, explain why this view is inaccurate.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks for a developed answer that: names at least one composer or piece (for example Terry Riley's In C, Steve Reich's Music for 18 Musicians, John Adams' Short Ride in a Fast Machine); explains at least one process that changes the material over time (additive process, phasing, or gradual layering); explains that structure emerges from this process rather than being absent; uses correct technical vocabulary (pulse, cell, harmonic rhythm, hocket); is coherently expressed. Award holistically: 1-2 basic, 3-4 clear, 5-6 detailed and well-supported.

glossary_terms.definition: Music built from short repeated patterns, a steady pulse and gradual, rule-based change, rather than from themes and development.
A steady, unchanging beat that runs underneath the music, often continuing unbroken from start to end.
A short musical pattern, often only a bar or two long, that repeats far more than an ordinary motif.
A technique where notes are added to a repeating pattern one at a time, so the pattern grows longer with each repeat.
A technique where two identical parts start together, then one gradually shifts out of time with the other, creating new interlocking patterns.
Adding instrumental or vocal layers on top of an existing pattern one at a time, so the texture thickens gradually.
How often the underlying chord changes; slow harmonic rhythm means the same chord is held for a long time before it moves.
A technique where two parts interlock by alternating single notes, so neither part plays a full melody alone but the two together create one.
Another name for minimalism, describing music whose structure comes from following a process rather than developing a theme.
A structure built on two contrasting themes that are stated, developed and restated, used as the main contrast to minimalism in this course.

flashcard_questions.a: Music built from short repeated patterns, a steady pulse and gradual, rule-based change, rather than from themes and development.

A process in which notes are added to a repeating pattern one at a time so it grows longer with each repeat. In C does not use it: its 53 numbered patterns are fixed, and each player repeats one as often as they like before moving on, so the ensemble drifts in and out of step through staggered repetition instead.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the additive process, and does Terry Riley's In C use it?

flashcard_questions.a: Two identical parts start together in time, then one gradually pulls ahead until the lines lock into a new relationship; Steve Reich is known for it.
flashcard_questions.q: What is phasing, and which composer is known for it?

flashcard_questions.a: A technique in which two parts interlock by alternating single notes, so neither part plays a full melody alone but the two together create one.
Short Ride in a Fast Machine.
flashcard_questions.q: Which John Adams piece lasts about four minutes and is used as the clearest introduction to minimalist layering?
